Fleet managers are under pressure to keep costs down and vehicles running through disruptions and emissions requirements, often with the same budget. These goals can seem to compete. In practice, many of the smartest moves can achieve all three goals at once. Fuel that a fleet never burns costs nothing, emits nothing and can't run short.
Know where the pressure points are
What’s Related
Rising costs are the most visible pressure right now. The average cost to operate a truck in the U.S. hit a record $2.336 per mile in 2025, according to the American Transportation Research Institute.
Many carriers responded by cutting trucks and keeping older equipment. That saved money up front but came at a cost. Older trucks typically need more upkeep, and repair and maintenance costs rose 8.6% across the industry that year.
This is a useful lesson for supply chain teams in any region. A cut that helps one goal can quietly show up later as a cost against another.
RELATED STORIES: Trucking Rates Could Climb in 2027, Even Without More Freight to Move | The Top 10 Issues Facing the Trucking Industry in 2026
Match equipment to the real duty cycle
Smart fleet planning starts well before a vehicle hits the road. Fleets often grow over time to include units that are rarely used, highly specialized or poorly suited to current work. A duty cycle is how much and how often a vehicle works. The U.S. Department of Energy recommends reviewing each vehicle's duty cycle as part of a broader fleet review to identify these gaps.
A good review asks a few simple questions:
Use : What tasks does each unit perform, and how often?
Fit: Is it the right type, class and size for the job?
Condition: Is it still cost-effective to run, or does it spend too much time out of service?
Dan Parks
Sustainability and cost control begin with picking equipment that matches the fleet's actual duty cycle. An oversized engine can affect equipment balance and burn unnecessary fuel, while an undersized one strains under load and wears out sooner.
Wise fleet managers choose the right engine size to shape fuel use, productivity, durability, maintenance and downtime for years to come. That makes it one of the simplest ways for fleets to balance resilience , cost and sustainability from day one.
Cut idle time before adding new tech
Idling is one of the easiest losses to fix. Argonne National Laboratory estimates that idling long-haul trucks burn more than 1 billion gallons of fuel annually at required rest stops.
Less idling also supports resilience. The same DOE guidance links lower petroleum use to more flexibility during natural disasters and fuel supply disruptions.
A few practical steps can help:
Set clear idle rules: Give drivers simple guidance on when to shut down.
Use telematics data : Flag the units and routes with the most idle hours.
Add idle reduction equipment: Auxiliary battery packs and similar units can power heating and cooling without running the main engine.
Switch to drop-in fuels where supply allows
Lower-carbon fuel doesn't always mean new vehicles. Renewable diesel can run in existing engines without changes to vehicles, storage or fueling equipment. That's why it's often called drop-in fuel.
Oakland, California, offers a real-world example. The city began moving its diesel vehicles to renewable diesel in 2015 and now runs its entire diesel fleet on fuel made from waste cooking oil. Since the pilot began, the fleet has cut fine particle pollution by 33% and nitrogen oxides by 9%.
In the UK, Adur & Worthing Councils switched their waste and recycling trucks to hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) in July 2025. HVO is a renewable fuel made from waste materials. The councils say the switch has cut the service's carbon emissions by up to 90% .
Supply varies by region, though. Fleets should confirm steady local availability before switching fully, so a greener fuel doesn't become a new weak point.
How to measure progress
Tracking fuel use and emissions in one place shows which changes actually pay off. The EPA's SmartWay program gives carriers and shippers a common system to track and share this data.
The results add up. U.S. trucking companies using the program have saved $55.4 billion on fuel bills to date. SmartWay also serves as a model for green freight programs in other regions, which makes it a useful reference for global supply chains.
Build a fleet that holds up under pressure
Balancing resilience, cost and sustainability isn't about finding a perfect trade-off. It's about choosing moves that serve multiple goals. Right-sized equipment and less idling cut spending and emissions while making operations steadier. Fleets that start there build a stronger base for bigger changes later.
Dan Parks is a senior writer at Modded.com with six years of experience specializing in supply chain content.
